chunks: The Quran has spoken of what happened to the sons of Yaqub (peace be upon him) with their brother Yusuf (peace be upon him), how they threw him into the well and sold him for a low price, and they were the sons of the prophets, and among people there are those who say they were prophets. If such an act is permissible from them despite the greatness of the error therein, then why should it not be permissible for Ja'far ibn Ali regarding his nephew, and for him to do with him the denial out of greed for the world and attaining it? And who would prevent this except an obstinate opponent?

key_terms.جَعْفَرِ بْنِ عَلِيٍّ: Ja'far ibn Ali (peace be upon him)

ai.seo_question: Why is Ja'far ibn Ali's denial of his nephew's status considered permissible in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi employs a qiyas (analogical reasoning) to defend the legitimacy of the Imam's concealment (ghayba) by comparing it to the actions of the sons of Jacob, whom Shia tradition often regards as prophets. He argues that if the prophets committed significant errors like selling Joseph for a low price, then Ja'far al-Sadiq's denial of his nephew's imamate to avoid political persecution is a permissible, albeit lesser, act. This counters critics who view the Imam's concealment as an anomaly, framing it instead as a consistent theological precedent.
